scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did something wrong by keeping the $1100 I won at the family gathering. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, the family gatherings are a big deal. We have a lot of cousins, and we all live close, so getting together is common. My grandparents have a ranch where we usually meet, and these gatherings often involve sports, grilling, and gambling. I'm not really into gambling, but I participate to be social. Usually, I lose money because I don't know much about cards or sports teams. It's become a running joke among family members. This time, the gathering was especially large, so my aunt came up with a new idea to make things simpler. She filled a jar with beans and placed it on the mantle. She said it was $20 a guess, and whoever guessed closest to the number of beans would take home all the money. Almost everyone participated, and some even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Now, here's where I come in. I'm usually not good at gambling, but this time I felt like I was in my element. I knew the jar was a typical 64 oz Mason jar, which I quickly looked up and found out was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Dividing the jar's volume by the bean's volume gave me approximately 773 beans. Then, I assumed 20% of the jar was air, which left me with around 619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and another for 630. When I was making my bets, people were teasing me, saying things like, "It'd be easier if you just gave it directly to me," but I just smiled and didn't say anything. Some people could tell I was onto something and continued to tease me throughout the night. After about 40 minutes of counting, my aunt announced that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anyone else's. At first, everyone was happy for me, laughing about how lucky I was. But then one of the suspicious cousins asked me how I did it, and I told everyone my strategy. Immediately, I could see people's faces souring. One of my uncles said, "That's bullsh*t," and left the room. In the end, I ended up winning nearly $1100. My parents told me I should offer to return it because I didn't earn it fairly. I argued that I had all the same information as everyone else. Now, I'm wondering if I did something wrong by keeping the money. So, is it right or wrong for me to keep the money? Let's break this down. First, I used my knowledge of math and volume to estimate the number of beans in the jar. I made two guesses to increase my chances. I didn't cheat by looking at the jar or manipulating it in any way. I simply used information that was available to me, like the size of the jar and the volume of a bean. On the other hand, most of my family members didn't use this kind of strategy. They probably guessed randomly or based on other factors. My cousins and uncles didn't seem to know about the math behind it, and when I explained my strategy, they got upset. My parents think I should return the money because I didn't earn it fairly. But I believe I did earn it fairly because I used the same information everyone else had access to. I didn't have any unfair advantages. However, I can see why my family might feel upset. Gambling is supposed to be a social activity where everyone has an equal chance. By using a mathematical strategy, I might have skewed the odds in my favor, making it less fair for others. But wait, wasn't the game designed in a way that allowed people to make educated guesses? The aunt set it up as a guessing game, but she didn't specify that it had to be purely random. If someone could figure out the number of beans through calculation, that's technically within the rules. Still, the fact that my family was upset suggests that there's an implicit expectation that everyone should play on a level playing field. By using a strategy that others didn't, I might have violated that social contract. Moreover, the amount of money involved is significantâĢĶ$1100. That's a lot of money for a family gathering, and it's understandable that people would feel strongly about it. In the end, I have to weigh the fairness of the game against the social expectations of my family. Did I play by the rules? Yes. Did I have an unfair advantage? Maybe, because not everyone knew how to calculate the number of beans. Did I cheat? No, I didn't manipulate the jar or the game in any way. But if my family feels that I didn't play fairly, even if I technically followed the rules, then maybe I should consider returning the money to maintain harmony in the family. Alternatively, I could explain my strategy to my family and argue that I did play fairly, using the information available to me. This might help them understand that I didn't cheat, but it might not change their feelings about it. So, is it right or wrong for me to keep the money? It depends on how you define fairness. If fairness is about following the rules, then I did nothing wrong. If fairness is about ensuring everyone has an equal chance, then maybe I did have an unfair advantage. Given that my family is upset, it might be better to return the money to keep the peace, even if I believe I didn't do anything wrong. Relationships are important, and avoiding conflict might be worth more than the money. On the other hand, if I keep the money, I might be setting a precedent that using strategies to win is acceptable, which could lead to more competitive and less harmonious family gatherings in the future. In conclusion, while I didn't cheat, the situation has caused tension within the family. To maintain good relationships, it might be better to return the money, even if I believe I earned it fairly.
